title: Route header canonicalization bug led to cross-variant serve and stalled rollback
creator: Ava Chen
description: Summary: During a staged canary promotion of model v3.1 -> v3.2 we observed a routing mismatch caused by header canonicalization in the edge translator. Requests intended for the canary split (10%) were partially misrouted to the baseline variant due to duplicate header normalization (X-Route and x-route), which resulted in inconsistent KV cache keys and mixed-serve responses. Attempts to rollback were blocked by a pinned-version latch on several router instances, causing a ~42 minute period of high error variance and increased tail latency for affected customers. This ticket captures timeline, root cause analysis, mitigation, and action items.
incident_summary: At 02:14 UTC a canary swap began. At 02:18 we saw a spike in mismatched responses where single requests returned mixed variant outputs in downstream traces. At 02:27 the automated rollback started but several router nodes had pinlock on v3.2 and could not accept the rollback update, causing partial rollback and client-visible 500s. Full recovery completed at 03:01 after a forced unpin and controlled drain. Impact: 18 customers saw degraded outputs; 5 customers filed support tickets. Token error rate peaked at 7.4% (baseline 0.2%).

root_cause:
Multiple contributing factors:
1) Edge route translator performed header canonicalization that collapsed distinct routing headers (X-Route vs x-route) into the same normalized field, causing requests that relied on case-sensitive header variants to be routed to the wrong backend variant.
2) KV cache key schema used non-fully-qualified route identity (omitted normalized-header version) so cached prefixes could be replayed to the wrong variant.
3) Control-plane rollout state allowed 'pinned-version' to persist on router instances when apply-ack was not confirmed; the pin did not time out under partial apply failures resulting in a stuck rollback path.
4) Health check thresholds were tuned for throughput degradation and did not flag mixed-serve semantic regressions quickly enough.
mitigations: Immediate: Forced unpin + graceful drain on affected router instances to complete rollback and clear mixed-serving state
Short-term: Backfill a post-rollback verification job that validates variant-consistency via synthetic requests and KV cache key checks (staging rollout)
Short-term: Tighten canary health checks to include output-consistency regression signals (embedding similarity checks and deterministic hash tests)
Mid-term: Change KV cache key to include full route identity including normalized header fingerprint to avoid cross-variant cache collisions
Mid-term: Add explicit canonicalization contracts in edge translator with a compatibility mode flag for rollout testing
Long-term: Implement rollback fencing with a bounded pin TTL and coordinator-driven unpin retries with exponential backoff

postmortem_notes: Trade-offs: We previously favored header-normalization to simplify downstream rules, but this incident shows the importance of preserving identity when headers are used for routing. A compatibility flag gives us a migration path without breaking older routes.

Decision: Split rollout of canonicalization into three phases: (1) observability-only (show diffs), (2) compatibility flag on by default in staging, (3) global on with migration plan. Agreed by eng + product.
Follow-up: Revisit health-check SLOs to include semantic checks; product accepted small increase in canary time to ensure output stability.
